question: Which of the following is NOT a name by which the author of the Arthashastra is known?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sandrokottos.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Arthashastra, the Sanskrit treatise on politics and statecraft, was written by Kautilya, who is also called Chanakya and Vishnugupta; Sandrokottos is not his name (कौटिल्य = चाणक्य = विष्णुगुप्त)

 

• Sandrokottos is the name by which Greek and Latin writers referred to Chandragupta Maurya, the king whom Kautilya helped to the throne.

 

• Kautilya is traditionally described as the guide of Chandragupta in overthrowing the Nanda dynasty.

 

• The Arthashastra is a book on politics and administration, written in Sanskrit.

 

• Kautilya's Arthashastra is a Sanskrit treatise on politics and statecraft, and the Mauryan state described in it is a strong, spy-supported monarchy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Arthashastra, Indica and Mudrarakshasa are the three main literary sources for the Mauryan period.

 

• The Arthashastra gives the Saptanga (seven-limb) theory of the state.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Mauryan Empire.

 

• Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta also celebrates the role of Chanakya.

 

• The Greek form Sandrokottos was identified with Chandragupta by Sir William Jones, which helped fix the chronology of ancient India.

 

NOTE

 

• Kautilya (Option 2): Kautilya is the best-known name of the author of the Arthashastra, so it is certainly one of his names. Hence it cannot be the answer to a NOT question.

 

• Chanakya (Option 3): Chanakya is the popular name of the same minister and author. It is therefore a genuine alternative name and cannot be the odd one out.

 

• Vishnugupta (Option 4): Vishnugupta is the personal name of the same person, also used in tradition for Kautilya. It is therefore a valid name and not the exception.

question: Which of the following is the correct match of the literary source with its author?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indica - Megasthenes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indica was written by Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador at the court of Chandragupta Maurya, and describes Mauryan administration, especially of Pataliputra (इंडिका — मेगस्थनीज)

 

• The Arthashastra was written by Kautilya (Chanakya), while Mudrarakshasa is a Sanskrit drama by Vishakhadatta.

 

• The Kalpasutra was composed by the Jain monk Bhadrabahu, a guide of Chandragupta in his last days.

 

• These three works - Arthashastra, Indica, Mudrarakshasa - are the three main literary sources of Mauryan history.

 

• The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya, Indica to Megasthenes and Mudrarakshasa to Vishakhadatta; Kalpasutra belongs to Bhadrabahu of the Jain tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The original Indica is lost; it survives only in quotations by later Greek and Roman writers.

 

• Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador at the Mauryan court.

 

• Mudrarakshasa narrates how Chandragupta, helped by Kautilya, overthrew the Nandas.

 

• Bhadrabahu is associated with Jain tradition and Sravana Belgola.

 

• Bhadrabahu's Kalpasutra is a Jain text, and Jain tradition links its author with the migration of monks to the south.

 

NOTE

 

• Arthashastra - Megasthenes (Option 1): The Arthashastra is a Sanskrit work on politics by Kautilya, not by Megasthenes. Megasthenes wrote Indica, so this pair mixes up the two authors.

 

• Mudrarakshasa - Kautilya (Option 2): Mudrarakshasa is a Sanskrit historical drama by Vishakhadatta about Chanakya's political contest with the Nanda minister Rakshasa. Kautilya appears in it as a character and is the author of the Arthashastra, not of this play.

 

• Kalpasutra - Vishakhadatta (Option 3): The Kalpasutra is a Jain scripture traditionally ascribed to the Jain monk Bhadrabahu, who is linked with Chandragupta's last days. Vishakhadatta was a dramatist, so this pairing mixes up a religious text with a political play.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven essential elements (Saptanga) of the state described by Kautilya?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dharma.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kautilya's Saptanga Siddhanta names Raja/Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda and Mitra as the seven limbs of the state; Dharma is not one of them (सप्तांग सिद्धांत — राजा, अमात्य, जनपद, दुर्ग, कोष, दंड, मित्र)

 

• Kautilya compares the state to a living body in which each limb depends on the others.

 

• Danda stands for the army and Mitra for the ally, whereas Janapada means population and territory.

 

• The theory is found in the Arthashastra, the main text on Mauryan statecraft.

 

• The Saptanga theory treats the state as an organism, so the loss of any one limb such as the treasury or the army weakens the whole kingdom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raja or Swami is the sovereign; Amatya is the minister.

 

• Durga is the fortified capital and Kosha the treasury.

 

• The theory shows the Mauryan concept of a centralised monarchical state.

 

• The Arthashastra also discusses diplomacy and war in detail.

 

• Kautilya's list is sometimes remembered with the mnemonic Swami-Amatya-Janapada-Durga-Kosha-Danda-Mitra, which is the order given in the Arthashastra.

 

NOTE

 

• Amatya (Option 2): Amatya, meaning the minister, is a recognised limb of the state in the Saptanga theory. Hence it is a genuine element and not the answer.

 

• Kosha (Option 3): Kosha means the treasury and is the fifth limb of the Saptanga theory. It is therefore part of the list and cannot be the exception.

 

• Durga (Option 4): Durga means the fortified capital and is the fourth limb of the theory. Since it is a real element, it is not the odd one out.

question:
Match the elements of Kautilya's Saptanga theory with their meanings:

(a) Amatya  (i) The army

(b) Janapada  (ii) The minister

(c) Danda  (iii) The treasury

(d) Kosha  (iv) The population and territory
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Saptanga theory Amatya is the minister, Janapada is the population and territory, Danda is the army and Kosha is the treasury, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (अमात्य = मंत्री, जनपद = प्रजा व क्षेत्र, दंड = सेना, कोष = खजाना)

 

• The other limbs are Raja/Swami (sovereign), Durga (fortified capital) and Mitra (ally).

 

• Kautilya treats the state like a body whose seven parts depend on each other.

 

• This theory is part of the Arthashastra.

 

• The seven limbs are Raja/Swami, Amatya (minister), Janapada (population and territory), Durga (fortified capital), Kosha (treasury), Danda (army) and Mitra (ally).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Durga means a fortified capital or fort.

 

• The word Danda literally means punishment or force and stands for the army.

 

• Janapada in this context is not a Mahajanapada but the people and land of a state.

 

• Mitra is the ally who supports the king in war and diplomacy.

 

• The Arthashastra also lists six methods of foreign policy, such as peace and war, which complement the Saptanga theory.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This combination gives Amatya as the army and Janapada as the minister, which is wrong. Amatya is the minister and Janapada the population and territory.

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 2): This combination treats Amatya as the population and Janapada as the army, which is wrong. Amatya is the minister, Janapada is the population with its territory, and Danda is the army, while Kosha is the treasury.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 4): This combination treats Amatya as the army and Danda as the treasury, which is wrong. Danda is the army and Kosha is the treasury.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Indica of Megasthenes:

1. It describes Mauryan administration, especially the city administration of Pataliputra.

2. It records that the Mauryan Empire had a flourishing system of slavery.

3. It mentions a division of Indian society into seven groups.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 3 are correct: Indica describes Mauryan administration, especially Pataliputra, and divides Indian society into seven classes (इंडिका — पाटलिपुत्र प्रशासन, सात वर्ग)

 

• Statement 2 is wrong because Megasthenes recorded that there was no slavery in the Mauryan Empire.

 

• The seven divisions were philosophers, farmers, soldiers, herdsmen, artisans, magistrates and councillors.

 

• Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador sent to the court of Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• He also recorded the military organisation of the empire.

 

• Megasthenes also wrote that Indians were honest and that theft was rare, but SSC mainly asks about slavery, seven classes and Pataliputra.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The city of Pataliputra was run by six committees of five members each, according to Megasthenes.

 

• Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus Nicator.

 

• Indica survives only in fragments quoted by later writers.

 

• Kautilya's Arthashastra is the Indian source that complements Indica.

 

• Only fragments of Indica survive in the works of later writers like Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus, who quoted Megasthenes.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Statement 1 is true because Indica does describe Mauryan administration, but statement 2 is false, so this pair is incomplete. Megasthenes wrote that slavery did not exist in the Mauryan Empire, and also listed seven social divisions, which is statement 3.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Statement 3 is correct but statement 2 is wrong, so including it makes this combination incorrect. Megasthenes did not describe a flourishing slave system.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Statement 2 is false because Megasthenes recorded that slavery did not exist in Mauryan India. Hence the claim that all three are correct fails.

question: According to Megasthenes, the city administration of Pataliputra was conducted by six committees of how many members each?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 5.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Megasthenes recorded that the city administration of Pataliputra was run by six committees of 5 members each, i.e. 30 members in all (पाटलिपुत्र नगर प्रशासन — छह समितियाँ, प्रत्येक में 5 सदस्य)

 

• This account is preserved in his book Indica.

 

• It shows the organised and centralised nature of Mauryan urban administration.

 

• Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador at the court of Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• The five-member committees together had thirty members, and Greek accounts say they looked after matters such as foreigners, trade and public welfare.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan Empire.

 

• The Arthashastra mentions the Nagarika, the city superintendent, who maintained law and order.

 

• Indica also gave details of the military organisation.

 

• Megasthenes is said to have been sent by Seleucus Nicator.

 

• Pataliputra stood at the confluence of the Ganga and the Son, and Greek writers described it as a huge city with a wooden palisade.

 

NOTE

 

• 3 (Option 1): Three members per committee does not match the account of Megasthenes. He mentioned six committees, each of five members, so thirty members in all ran the municipal affairs of Pataliputra.

 

• 4 (Option 2): Four is wrong as the size of each committee. Megasthenes described a board of six committees with five members each, which together managed city functions like crafts, foreigners, trade and tax collection at Pataliputra.

 

• 6 (Option 4): Six is the number of committees, not the number of members in each committee. This option confuses the count of committees with their size.

question: The Sanskrit drama 'Mudrarakshasa', which tells how Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas with the help of Kautilya, was written by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vishakhadatta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mudrarakshasa is a Sanskrit drama by Vishakhadatta that narrates how Chandragupta, helped by Kautilya, brought down the Nandas (मुद्राराक्षस — विशाखदत्त)

 

• It is counted among the three chief literary sources for the Mauryan period, along with the Arthashastra and Indica.

 

• The play is a source for the rise of Chandragupta and the role of Chanakya.

 

• The last Nanda ruler overthrown was Dhanananda.

 

• Mudrarakshasa is built around the political rivalry between Chanakya and the Nanda minister Rakshasa, which makes it a lively source for the Mauryan rise.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dhanananda was the last Nanda ruler.

 

• Chandragupta took Pataliputra when he was about twenty-five years old, according to the notes.

 

• Vishakhadatta also wrote the play Devichandraguptam, according to tradition.

 

• Literary sources must be combined with inscriptions for a full history.

 

• Vishakhadatta's play is a historical drama in Sanskrit and was probably written centuries after the Mauryan period.

 

NOTE

 

• Bhasa (Option 2): Bhasa was an early Sanskrit dramatist known for plays on epic and legendary themes such as Svapnavasavadatta. He lived long before Vishakhadatta and did not write the Mauryan political drama Mudrarakshasa.

 

• Kalidasa (Option 3): Kalidasa, the famous poet of the Gupta age, wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta and Raghuvamsa. He is not the author of Mudrarakshasa, which is a political drama by Vishakhadatta about Chandragupta and Chanakya.

 

• Banabhatta (Option 4): Banabhatta was the court poet of Harshavardhana in the 7th century AD and wrote Harshacharita and Kadambari. He lived many centuries after the Mauryas and did not write the drama Mudrarakshasa.

question: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire in about which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 322 BC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire in about 322 BC after taking Pataliputra from Dhanananda, the last Nanda ruler (चंद्रगुप्त मौर्य — मौर्य साम्राज्य की स्थापना, लगभग 322 ई.पू.)

 

• Some sources give 321 BC or 324 BC, so SSC options usually give only one of these dates.

 

• He was guided by Kautilya (Chanakya).

 

• The Mauryan Empire lasted from about 322 BC to 185 BC.

 

• The founding of the empire is placed in 322 BC in the notes, but 321 BC and 324 BC are also given in different books; SSC options usually offer only one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta was around twenty-five when he seized Pataliputra, according to the notes.

 

• Greek writers called him Sandrokottos.

 

• The dynasty ended with Brihadratha, killed by Pushyamitra Sunga in 185 BC.

 

• He defeated Seleucus Nicator in about 305 BC.

 

• Chandragupta's empire reached from Afghanistan in the north-west to Bengal in the east and into the Deccan.

 

NOTE

 

• 261 BC (Option 1): 261 BC is the year of the Kalinga War of Ashoka, not the founding of the empire. It is a landmark in Ashoka's reign.

 

• 273 BC (Option 3): 273 BC is traditionally the beginning of Ashoka's reign according to the notes. It is not the date of Chandragupta's founding of the empire.

 

• 185 BC (Option 4): 185 BC is the year in which the Mauryan dynasty ended, when Brihadratha was killed by his commander Pushyamitra Sunga. It marks the end of the empire and not its founding by Chandragupta.

question: Who was the last Nanda ruler, from whom Chandragupta Maurya took Pataliputra?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dhanananda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dhanananda was the last Nanda ruler, and Chandragupta Maurya took Pataliputra from him with the help of Kautilya (धनानंद — अंतिम नंद शासक)

 

• The event is described in the play Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta.

 

• Chandragupta was only about 25 years old at that time, according to the class notes.

 

• With this victory the Mauryan Empire was established in about 322 BC.

 

• Dhanananda was unpopular because of heavy taxes, which is one reason traditional accounts give for the ease with which Chandragupta replaced him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Nandas preceded the Mauryas in Magadha.

 

• Chandragupta's empire later extended to the Hindu Kush.

 

• Chanakya is credited with planning the downfall of the Nandas.

 

• Pataliputra remained the Mauryan capital.

 

• The Nandas, beginning with Mahapadma Nanda, were the first non-Kshatriya dynasty in Magadha according to tradition.

 

• Pataliputra, which Chandragupta captured, was earlier the Nanda capital and remained the Mauryan capital throughout the dynasty.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahapadma Nanda (Option 1): Mahapadma Nanda was the founder of the Nanda dynasty and ruled long before Chandragupta, who overthrew Dhanananda. He is therefore the first Nanda king and not the last one displaced by the Mauryas.

 

• Bimbisara (Option 2): Bimbisara was an early king of Magadha belonging to the Haryanka dynasty, who married a Kosalan princess and conquered Anga. He ruled around the 6th century BC, much before the Nandas and the Mauryas.

 

• Brihadratha (Option 3): Brihadratha was the last king of the Mauryan dynasty who was killed by his general Pushyamitra Sunga. He belonged to the Mauryan line and not to the Nandas, whom Chandragupta had overthrown long before.

question: In 305 BC Chandragupta Maurya marched against Seleucus Nicator. Which of the following was the outcome?
option_1: Seleucus gave up Aria, Arachosia and Gedrosia and gave his daughter in marriage to the Mauryan prince
option_2: Chandragupta was defeated and lost Pataliputra
option_3: The Mauryas gave 500 elephants and received Bactria in return
option_4: The two kings divided Punjab equally
solution_text:
The correct answer is Seleucus gave up Aria, Arachosia and Gedrosia and gave his daughter in marriage to the Mauryan prince.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta won the war of 305 BC and Seleucus Nicator handed over Aria, Arachosia and Gedrosia, also marrying his daughter to the Mauryan prince (सेल्यूकस निकेटर संधि — 305 ई.पू.)

 

• In return Chandragupta gave Seleucus 500 elephants, which later helped Seleucus at Ipsus.

 

• Most of Afghanistan up to the Hindu Kush came to Chandragupta as part of the settlement.

 

• Megasthenes was sent as Greek ambassador to the Mauryan court after this treaty.

 

• The Mauryan victory is remembered as a rare case in which an Indian ruler defeated a Greek successor of Alexander in the field.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Seleucus Nicator had been Alexander's general and held the north-west of India.

 

• The treaty brought a long period of peaceful relations with the Greek world.

 

• Bindusara later received Deimachus as ambassador from Antiochus I.

 

• Chandragupta's empire thus extended from Bengal to Afghanistan.

 

• The Mauryan-Seleucid friendship continued, and the Greek envoy Megasthenes lived at Pataliputra for several years.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandragupta was defeated and lost Pataliputra (Option 2): Chandragupta won the war of 305 BC, so the claim of defeat is wrong. He gained territories up to the Hindu Kush by the treaty and kept Pataliputra, and his empire was strengthened by the peace settlement.

 

• The Mauryas gave 500 elephants and received Bactria in return (Option 3): The elephants were given by Chandragupta to Seleucus, but Seleucus did not give Bactria. Bactria is not among the territories transferred in the treaty.

 

• The two kings divided Punjab equally (Option 4): The treaty did not divide Punjab equally between the two kings. Seleucus handed over the territories of Aria, Arachosia and Gedrosia, received 500 elephants in return, and Chandragupta clearly emerged as the winner.

question: Towards the end of his life Chandragupta Maurya adopted Jainism under the influence of Bhadrabahu. Where did he observe Sallekhana (ritual fasting until death)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sravana Belgola.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chandragupta gave up the throne to Bindusara, travelled with Jain monks led by Bhadrabahu to Sravana Belgola in Karnataka and observed Sallekhana (श्रवणबेलगोला — सल्लेखना, भद्रबाहु)

 

• Bhadrabahu is the author of the Kalpasutra.

 

• Sallekhana is the Jain practice of ritual fasting until death.

 

• Sravana Belgola is near Mysore in Karnataka.

 

• Sallekhana, voluntary fasting to death, is a Jain practice also known as Santhara, which the notes link to the last days of Chandragupta.

 

• The notes add that the 1st Jain council is said to have been held during Chandragupta's reign, which links him closely with early Jain tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The 1st Jain council is said to have been held during his reign.

 

• Chandragupta's son Bindusara followed the Ajivika sect.

 

• Sravana Belgola later became famous for the Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue.

 

• Chandragupta's Jain connection is also reflected in Jain tradition.

 

• Sravana Belgola in Karnataka later became a major Jain centre with the colossal Gomateshwara statue, built in the 10th century AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Udayagiri (Option 1): Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar in Odisha is a Jain-Buddhist cave site famous for Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription. It has no link with Chandragupta's Sallekhana, which happened at Sravana Belgola in Karnataka.

 

• Girnar (Option 2): Girnar in Gujarat is a hill near Junagarh associated with the Sudarshana lake, Rudradaman's inscription and Ashoka's rock edicts. Chandragupta's Sallekhana is not placed here but at Sravana Belgola in Karnataka.

 

• Mount Abu (Option 3): Mount Abu in Rajasthan is known for the Dilwara Jain temples, built many centuries after the Mauryas. It has no connection with Chandragupta, who observed Sallekhana at Sravana Belgola near Mysore.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Junagarh (Girnar) inscription:

1. It was issued by the Saka ruler Rudradaman.

2. It is the first long inscription in Sanskrit.

3. It records the construction of the Sudarshana lake during the reign of Ashoka.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Junagarh (Girnar) inscription was issued by the Saka king Rudradaman and is the first long Sanskrit inscription (जूनागढ़ अभिलेख — रुद्रदामन, सुदर्शन झील)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong in the way it is phrased: the inscription speaks of the Sudarshana lake built in the time of Chandragupta Maurya, with governor Pushyagupta.

 

• It is located in Kathiawar, Gujarat, and is also called the Girnar or Rudradaman inscription.

 

• It gives information about both the lake and Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Rudradaman was a Saka ruler, not a Mauryan.

 

• The Junagarh inscription is dated about AD 150 in the reign of Rudradaman, which shows that the Saka rulers of western India used refined Sanskrit.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pushyagupta was Chandragupta's governor who built the lake.

 

• Later rulers repaired the lake, and Rudradaman recorded its repair.

 

• The Junagarh rock also carries Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts.

 

• Sanskrit inscriptions became common after this period.

 

• The same rock at Junagarh also has a set of Ashoka's fourteen Major Rock Edicts, and later a Gupta inscription of Skandagupta.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This combination includes statement 3 but leaves out statement 1. Rudradaman, a Saka king, did issue the inscription, so statement 1 is true and this option fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This combination also relies on statement 3, which wrongly attributes the lake to Ashoka. The inscription links the Sudarshana lake with Chandragupta Maurya, so statement 3 is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Statement 3 attributes the lake to Ashoka, which is wrong. The notes link the Sudarshana lake with Chandragupta Maurya, so not all three can be correct.

question: The Sudarshana lake in Gujarat was built during the reign of Chandragupta Maurya with the help of which governor?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pushyagupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pushyagupta, the governor of Chandragupta Maurya in the western region, built the Sudarshana lake (सुदर्शन झील — पुष्यगुप्त वैश्य)

 

• The Junagarh inscription of Rudradaman gives information about both the lake and Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• The lake was built for irrigation in the Girnar region of Gujarat.

 

• The inscription is the first long Sanskrit inscription.

 

• The Sudarshana lake served the Girnar region as a major irrigation reservoir, which shows the Mauryan state's interest in public works.

 

• The Junagarh inscription is the source that connects the Sudarshana lake with both Chandragupta Maurya and his governor Pushyagupta, so it is a key Mauryan source.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The lake was later repaired during the Saka rule of Rudradaman.

 

• The Sudarshana lake is the best-known Mauryan irrigation work.

 

• Tushaspa was a Yavana governor under Ashoka who built canals there.

 

• Girnar is near Junagarh in Gujarat.

 

• The lake burst its dam in a storm and was repaired in the time of Rudradaman and again in the Gupta period under Skandagupta.

 

NOTE

 

• Pushyamitra (Option 1): Pushyamitra Sunga killed the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha in 185 BC. He is a later figure and has nothing to do with the lake.

 

• Rudradaman (Option 2): Rudradaman was a Saka ruler of western India who issued the Junagarh inscription centuries later. He recorded the repair of the Sudarshana lake but did not build it, as it was built under Chandragupta by Pushyagupta.

 

• Tushaspa (Option 3): Tushaspa was a Yavana governor of Ashoka mentioned in the inscription for the canals. The lake was built under Chandragupta by Pushyagupta, not by him.

question:
Match the personalities with their descriptions:

(a) Bhadrabahu  (i) Seleucid envoy at the court of Bindusara

(b) Deimachus  (ii) Jain monk who guided Chandragupta in his last days

(c) Upagupta  (iii) Governor who built the Sudarshana lake

(d) Pushyagupta  (iv) Buddhist monk who influenced Ashoka
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bhadrabahu guided Chandragupta (Jain monk), Deimachus was the envoy of Antiochus I at Bindusara's court, Upagupta influenced Ashoka's conversion and Pushyagupta built the Sudarshana lake, so a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (भद्रबाहु, डायमेकस, उपगुप्त, पुष्यगुप्त)

 

• Bhadrabahu composed the Kalpasutra.

 

• Upagupta was the Buddhist monk under whose influence Ashoka embraced Buddhism after Kalinga.

 

• Deimachus came to the Mauryan court from the Syrian king Antiochus I.

 

• Bhadrabahu was a Jain monk, Deimachus the envoy of Antiochus I, Upagupta a Buddhist monk and Pushyagupta the governor under whom the lake was built.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Megasthenes was the ambassador of Seleucus at Chandragupta's court.

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa presided over the Third Buddhist Council.

 

• Sudarshana lake is described in the Junagarh inscription.

 

• Bindusara asked Antiochus I for wine, figs and a sophist.

 

• Megasthenes, Deimachus and Dionysius are the best-known Greek envoys at Mauryan courts mentioned in tradition.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 2): This matching reverses the roles of Bhadrabahu and Deimachus with others. Bhadrabahu was a Jain monk, not a Seleucid envoy, so it is wrong.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 3): This combination links Bhadrabahu with the governor who built the lake and Upagupta with the Jain monk, which is wrong. Bhadrabahu was the Jain monk and Upagupta a Buddhist monk.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 4): This matching pairs Deimachus with the lake and Pushyagupta with the Seleucid envoy, which is incorrect. Deimachus was the envoy and Pushyagupta the governor.

question: Bindusara, the son of Chandragupta Maurya, was a follower of which religious sect?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ajivika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bindusara supported the Ajivikas and was himself a follower of Ajivikism (आजीविक संप्रदाय — बिंदुसार)

 

• His father Chandragupta turned to Jainism in old age, while his son Ashoka later embraced Buddhism.

 

• Bindusara ruled from about 298 BC to 273 BC.

 

• He appointed Ashoka as the governor of Ujjain.

 

• Ajivika was an ascetic sect founded by Makkhali Gosala and was a rival of Buddhism and Jainism in the Mauryan period.

 

• The notes also state that Bindusara appointed Ashoka governor of Ujjain, and that the Amatyas revolted at Taxila during his reign before Ashoka put it down.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ajivikism was a sect associated with Makkhali Gosala.

 

• Ashoka later gave cave dwellings to Ajivikas in the Barabar hills.

 

• Bindusara maintained good relations with the Greek world.

 

• His reign saw a revolt at Taxila.

 

• Ashoka and later his grandson Dasharatha donated cave dwellings in the Barabar hills to Ajivika monks.

 

NOTE

 

• Jainism (Option 1): Jainism was adopted by Chandragupta Maurya towards the end of his life under Bhadrabahu, and not by his son Bindusara. The notes record Bindusara as a patron and follower of the Ajivikas, a rival ascetic sect.

 

• Buddhism (Option 2): Buddhism was embraced by Ashoka after the Kalinga War under the influence of Upagupta, not by his father Bindusara. Bindusara supported the Ajivikas, so this option confuses the faith of father and son.

 

• Charvaka (Option 4): Charvaka was a materialist school of thought and not a religious sect supported by the Mauryan rulers. The notes record Bindusara as an Ajivika follower.

question: Bindusara wrote to Antiochus I asking for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist. Which of these did Antiochus I NOT send?
solution_text:
The correct answer is A sophist.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Antiochus I of Syria sent the sweet wine and dried figs but refused to send the sophist, because Greek law did not permit the sale of a sophist (सोफिस्ट — यूनानी दार्शनिक)

 

• The exchange shows cordial diplomatic relations between the Mauryas and the Seleucid world.

 

• Deimachus was received by Bindusara as the ambassador of Antiochus I.

 

• Bindusara ruled from about 298 to 273 BC.

 

• Greek law forbade the sale of a sophist, so the refusal is a mark of diplomatic politeness and not of hostility between the two courts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta had earlier defeated Seleucus Nicator, the father of Antiochus I.

 

• Megasthenes served under Chandragupta, Deimachus under Bindusara.

 

• Trade between India and the Hellenistic world continued in this period.

 

• Bindusara's reign also saw a revolt at Taxila.

 

• Antiochus I was the son of Seleucus Nicator, who had made the treaty with Chandragupta.

 

NOTE

 

• Sweet wine (Option 1): Sweet wine was among the items sent by Antiochus I to Bindusara, so it is not the one refused. The only thing he did not send was the sophist, since Greek law did not allow a sophist to be sold.

 

• Dried figs (Option 2): Dried figs were sent by Antiochus I along with the wine, as Bindusara had requested. The single item withheld was the sophist, so figs cannot be the answer to a question on what was not sent.

 

• Both wine and figs (Option 3): Both the wine and the figs reached Bindusara from Antiochus I, so this option describes what was sent. Only the sophist was withheld, because Greek law did not permit his sale, which shows diplomatic courtesy.

question:
Consider the following statements about Ashoka before he became king:

1. He served as the governor of Ujjain during Bindusara's reign.

2. He crushed a revolt at Taxila by the Amatyas.

3. He was the governor of Kalinga at that time.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Ashoka was governor of Ujjain under Bindusara and put down the Taxila revolt, a revolt by the Amatyas (उज्जैन का गवर्नर, तक्षशिला विद्रोह)

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: Kalinga was conquered by him in 261 BC after he became king and was not his governorship.

 

• The revolt at Taxila was by the Amatyas, the highest officials.

 

• Ashoka ruled from about 273 BC (traditional date) to 232 BC.

 

• Ashoka's early career as governor of Ujjain and as the suppressor of the Taxila revolt prepared him for the throne after Bindusara.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ujjain was one of the four provincial capitals of the empire.

 

• The provinces were Taxila, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Kalinga.

 

• Provincial governors were usually chosen from the royal family.

 

• Ashoka's succession was disputed.

 

• Ashoka's own Rock Edict mentions brothers as officers, so the chronicle story of mass killing is doubtful.

 

• The Ceylonese chronicles Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa say Ashoka was called Chandashoka before his conversion and Dharmashoka afterwards.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This choice includes the false statement 3 but leaves out statement 1. Ashoka was governor of Ujjain, so statement 1 is true and the option fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This choice also depends on the false statement 3 and leaves out statement 1, which is true. Kalinga was a later conquest and not his governorship.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Statement 3 is wrong because Kalinga was conquered by Ashoka in 261 BC after he became king; it was not his governorship before accession. Only Ujjain and the Taxila revolt belong to his early career, so all three cannot be true.

question:
Arrange the following Mauryan rulers in chronological order:

1. Ashoka  2. Chandragupta Maurya  3. Brihadratha  4. Bindusara
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2, 4, 1, 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct order is Chandragupta Maurya (322-298 BC), Bindusara (298-273 BC), Ashoka (273-232 BC) and Brihadratha, the last ruler (मौर्य शासकों का क्रम — चंद्रगुप्त, बिंदुसार, अशोक, बृहद्रथ)

 

• Brihadratha was killed by his commander Pushyamitra Sunga.

 

• The empire lasted from about 322 BC to 185 BC.

 

• Each ruler was the father or ancestor of the next in the line.

 

• The reign periods in the notes are Chandragupta 322-298 BC, Bindusara 298-273 BC and Ashoka 273-232 BC; the last king Brihadratha ruled till 185 BC.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Chandragupta founded the empire; Bindusara expanded it; Ashoka was the greatest ruler.

 

• The dates of the reigns follow the class notes.

 

• Pushyamitra Sunga founded the Sunga dynasty.

 

• Pataliputra was the capital throughout.

 

• Ashoka is said to have been succeeded by his grandson Dasharatha according to the Puranas.

 

• The empire reached its largest extent under Ashoka, covering almost the whole subcontinent except the far south and parts of the north-east.

 

NOTE

 

• 4, 2, 1, 3 (Option 1): This order puts Bindusara before Chandragupta. Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire in about 322 BC and was succeeded by his son Bindusara in about 298 BC, so the sequence is incorrect.

 

• 2, 1, 4, 3 (Option 2): This order places Ashoka before Bindusara, but Bindusara was Ashoka's father and ruled from about 298 to 273 BC. Ashoka followed him on the throne, so Bindusara comes earlier in the correct order.

 

• 2, 4, 3, 1 (Option 3): This order places Ashoka after Brihadratha. Brihadratha was the last Mauryan king, killed by Pushyamitra Sunga in 185 BC, so he must come at the end of the list, long after Ashoka.

question: The Ceylonese Chronicles claim that Ashoka seized power after killing ninety-nine of his brothers. Which brother was spared?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tissa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa, Ashoka killed ninety-nine brothers, including the elder brother Susima, and spared only the youngest brother, Tissa (दीपवंश, महावंश — तिष्य बचाया गया)

 

• Taranatha of Tibet says he killed only six brothers.

 

• Ashoka's own edict mentions his brothers working as officers, so the story is doubtful.

 

• It is clear that his succession was disputed.

 

• The Ceylonese Chronicles are Buddhist sources from Sri Lanka, so they stress Ashoka's early cruelty and later piety, and historians use them with caution.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Ceylonese chronicles are Buddhist texts from Sri Lanka.

 

• They describe Ashoka as Chandashoka before his conversion.

 

• Mahendra and Sanghamitra were Ashoka's children sent to Sri Lanka.

 

• Susima was Ashoka's eldest brother.

 

• Taranatha was a Tibetan Buddhist monk of the 16th-17th century, whose account is much later than Ashoka's time.

 

NOTE

 

• Susima (Option 1): Susima was the elder brother of Ashoka and is said in the chronicles to have been killed in the struggle for the throne. He was therefore not the sibling who was spared, who was the youngest brother Tissa.

 

• Mahendra (Option 2): Mahendra was Ashoka's own son, who later led the Buddhist mission to Sri Lanka along with his sister Sangamitra. He was not among the brothers killed or spared in the succession story of the Ceylonese chronicles.

 

• Upagupta (Option 4): Upagupta was the Buddhist monk whose influence led Ashoka to embrace Buddhism after the Kalinga War. He was a monk and religious guide and not a brother of Ashoka, so he is not part of the succession story.

question: In his Maski inscription in Karnataka, Ashoka calls himself by which names?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Devanampriya and Priyadarshi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Maski inscription (Karnataka) Ashoka calls himself Devanampriya or Priyadarshi - the beautiful one beloved by the gods - and also Buddha Shakya (मास्की अभिलेख — देवानांप्रिय, प्रियदर्शी)

 

• The Maski inscription is important because it contains the personal name Ashoka.

 

• In the Sarnath pillar he is called Dharmasoka.

 

• It also names him Buddha Shakya.

 

• The Maski edict is a Minor Rock Edict and is important because it gives Ashoka's personal name, linking the title Devanampriya Priyadarsi with Ashoka.

 

• This inscription is a source for the Kalinga region and complements Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII, so the two together are cited for the Kalinga War.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Most of his edicts use the title Devanampriya Priyadarsi without his name.

 

• The Maski inscription confirms he was a Buddhist.

 

• The inscriptions are in Prakrit and mainly Brahmi script.

 

• Ashoka's edicts have been found from Afghanistan to Karnataka.

 

• The Maski edict was discovered in 1915 in the Raichur district of Karnataka.

 

NOTE

 

• Dharmasoka only (Option 2): Dharmasoka is the name by which Ashoka is called in the Sarnath pillar inscription. In the Maski inscription of Karnataka he describes himself as Devanampriya and Priyadarshi and also as Buddha Shakya, so this is not the answer.

 

• Chandashoka (Option 3): Chandashoka, meaning Ashoka the fierce, is a name from Buddhist tradition applied to his early cruel phase. It does not occur in the Maski inscription, which uses the titles Devanampriya and Priyadarshi.

 

• Samudragupta (Option 4): Samudragupta was a Gupta emperor of the 4th century AD, known for the Allahabad Pillar Prashasti. He lived nearly six centuries after Ashoka and has no connection with the Maski inscription of Karnataka.

question: The Hathigumpha cave inscription, a source for the Kalinga region, was issued by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kharavela.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hathigumpha cave inscription was issued by the Kalinga king Kharavela and is a source for Kalinga history, including the Mauryan connection (हाथीगुम्फा अभिलेख — खारवेल)

 

• Along with Rock Edict XIII, it is a source for the Kalinga War.

 

• It is located near Bhubaneswar in Odisha.

 

• Kalinga is present-day Odisha.

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription is a long record in the Brahmi script carved in a natural cave on Udayagiri hill near Bhubaneswar.

 

• The edict makes the Kalinga War the turning point of Ashoka's reign, since it led him toward Buddhism and the policy of Dhamma instead of conquest.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rudradaman issued the Junagarh inscription.

 

• Ashoka himself described the effects of the war in Rock Edict XIII.

 

• Samudragupta's Allahabad Prashasti was written by Harishena.

 

• Kharavela belonged to the Chedi dynasty of Kalinga.

 

• Kharavela of Kalinga, the issuer of this inscription, belonged to the Chedi dynasty and is dated to around the 1st century BC.

 

NOTE

 

• Rudradaman (Option 1): Rudradaman was the Saka ruler of western India who issued the Junagarh inscription in Gujarat. That record concerns the Sudarshana lake and Chandragupta Maurya, and it is not linked with Kalinga or with Hathigumpha.

 

• Ashoka (Option 3): Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII describes the effects of the Kalinga War, but the Hathigumpha inscription itself was not issued by him. It was issued by Kharavela of Kalinga, who ruled in the post-Mauryan period.

 

• Samudragupta (Option 4): Samudragupta is known for the Allahabad Pillar inscription composed by Harishena and belonged to the Gupta dynasty. He lived several centuries after Kharavela and has no connection with the Hathigumpha inscription.

question: Ashoka himself described the effects of the Kalinga War in which of his inscriptions?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Major Rock Edict XIII.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The effects of the Kalinga War (261 BC) are described by Ashoka himself in Major Rock Edict XIII, which expresses his deep remorse over the deaths and suffering of the war (१३वाँ शिलालेख — कलिंग युद्ध)

 

• The notes say that we have no details of why the war began or how it was fought, so the 13th edict is the main source on its effects.

 

• The edict records that Ashoka turned away from conquest by war and chose conquest by Dhamma.

 

• The Kalinga region is present-day Odisha, and the war is regarded as the most important event of Ashoka's reign.

 

• Rock Edict XIII is also the edict in which Ashoka mentions Greek kings such as Antiochus as neighbours reached by his Dhamma.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is another source on Kalinga.

 

• The war led to the adoption of Buddhism by Ashoka under the influence of Upagupta.

 

• After the war the emperor abandoned hunting tours and began Dhamma yatras.

 

• Ashoka's Dhamma later reached Sri Lanka and other countries through missions.

 

• Edict XIII reports that about 100,000 were killed, 150,000 deported and many more died in the Kalinga War.

 

NOTE

 

• Major Rock Edict IV (Option 1): Major Rock Edict IV does record the change from the war-drum to the Dhamma-drum, but it is not the edict that describes the effects of the Kalinga War. That description is in Edict XIII.

 

• Sarnath Pillar Edict (Option 2): The Sarnath pillar edict is mainly about maintaining unity in the Buddhist Sangha and does not describe the Kalinga War. The notes link the war's effects to Rock Edict XIII.

 

• Minor Rock Edict at Maski (Option 4): The Maski minor rock edict is important because it names Ashoka, but it does not describe the Kalinga War. Its significance lies in the personal title and name it gives.

question: After the Kalinga War, Ashoka abandoned the policy of Bherighosha and adopted which policy?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dhammaghosha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the Kalinga War of 261 BC, Ashoka gave up Bherighosha (conquest by the war-drum) and adopted Dhammaghosha (conquest by Dhamma), as recorded in his edicts (भेरीघोष से धम्मघोष)

 

• This change is mentioned in the 4th inscription according to the class notes.

 

• The new policy meant winning people through righteous conduct, respect for elders, non-violence and tolerance instead of through war.

 

• Ashoka also appointed Dhamma Mahamatras to spread the principles of Dhamma through the empire.

 

• The change from Bherighosha to Dhammaghosha is the standard SSC phrase for the Kalinga turning point in Ashoka's policy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The change of policy was caused by the horrors of the Kalinga War.

 

• Ashoka gave up hunting and went to Bodh Gaya after becoming a Buddhist.

 

• He sent missions to Sri Lanka and other lands to spread Dhamma.

 

• Dhamma was not a new religion but a code of conduct for all subjects.

 

• Ashoka still retained the army and the forest tribes were warned, so his non-violence was a moral policy rather than disarmament.

 

NOTE

 

• Digvijaya (Option 2): Digvijaya means conquest of the quarters by force of arms, which is the policy Ashoka gave up after Kalinga. It is the opposite of the new policy.

 

• Moksha (Option 3): Moksha means spiritual liberation, a goal of Buddhist and Jain teaching, but it was not the name of Ashoka's state policy. His policy was Dhammaghosha.

 

• Danda (Option 4): Danda stands for the army or punishment, which is one of the seven limbs of the state in the Arthashastra. It is not the post-Kalinga policy of Ashoka.

question: Under the influence of which Buddhist monk did Ashoka embrace Buddhism after the Kalinga War?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Upagupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War under the influence of the Buddhist monk Upagupta, according to the class notes (उपगुप्त — अशोक के बौद्ध गुरु)

 

• Around 261 BC he became a Sakya Upasaka, a lay follower, and two and a half years later a Bikshu, a monk.

 

• He then gave up hunting, went to Bodh Gaya and organised missions.

 

• The notes also say he appointed Dharma Mahamatras to push forward the progress of Dhamma.

 

• The notes mention that Ashoka first became a lay follower and then a monk about two and a half years later, showing a gradual religious journey.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa presided over the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra in 250 BC.

 

• Mahendra, Ashoka's son, led the mission to Sri Lanka.

 

• Bhadrabahu was the Jain monk linked with Chandragupta.

 

• Buddhist tradition names other monks as well, but SSC follows the notes.

 

• Buddhist tradition also gives the name Nigrodha, a young monk, as the one who first influenced Ashoka.

 

NOTE

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa (Option 1): Moggaliputta Tissa presided over the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra and is not the monk named in the notes for Ashoka's conversion. His role came later, in 250 BC.

 

• Mahendra (Option 3): Mahendra was Ashoka's son who led the Buddhist mission to Sri Lanka together with Sangamitra. He was a missionary of the later phase, and not the monk under whose influence Ashoka himself became a Buddhist.

 

• Bhadrabahu (Option 4): Bhadrabahu was a Jain monk, the author of the Kalpasutra, who guided Chandragupta Maurya. He had nothing to do with Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism.

question: Which of the following officers did Ashoka appoint to push forward the progress of Dhamma?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dhamma Mahamatras.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ashoka appointed special officers called Dhamma Mahamatras to promote the progress of Dhamma among all sections of society (धम्म महामात्र — धम्म प्रचार अधिकारी)

 

• These officers supervised the welfare of people and the spread of the moral principles stated in the edicts.

 

• Ashoka's Dhamma included service to parents, ahimsa, truth, respect to teachers and tolerance among sects.

 

• Dhamma Mahamatras were a new class of officers created by Ashoka and were additional to the normal civil servants called Amatyas.

 

• These officers were introduced in about the 13th year of Ashoka's reign and looked after all sects including Brahmins, Ajivikas and Jains.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rajukas were district officials similar to a modern collector.

 

• The Samharta headed the revenue department.

 

• The Nagarika was the city superintendent, discussed in the Arthashastra.

 

• The Amatyas were civil servants comparable to IAS officers.

 

• Ashoka also appointed Rajukas and Pradesikas who toured the realm and spread the message of Dhamma.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajukas (Option 1): Rajukas were district administrators comparable to a modern collector and were assisted by junior officials called Yuktas. Their role was general district administration and not the specific promotion of Dhamma.

 

• Samharta (Option 2): The Samharta headed the revenue department and was responsible for collecting all the revenue of the empire, such as land revenue and Sita land income. He was a fiscal official with no role in propagating Dhamma.

 

• Nagarika (Option 4): The Nagarika was the city superintendent whose main duty was the maintenance of law and order in the city. He was not an officer for spreading Dhamma.
